questions.question: How many types of EEG montages could be used?
options: Three: bipolar, referential and double banana montages
There are as many montages as electrodes within an EEG
questions.explanation: Two montage types are used in EEG: bipolar and referential montages.

questions.question: How can sedation affect the EEG recording?
options: Agents such as propofol may show fast activities, followed by progressive slowing to burst-suppression and eventually total suppression.
Volatile anaesthetics, propofol and barbiturates will cause progressive slowing and eventual burst-suppression
Dexmedetomidine may cause a pattern of slow-wave sleep.
questions.explanation: All of the listed effects are correct: propofol may produce fast activity followed by progressive slowing to burst-suppression and eventual total suppression; volatile anaesthetics, propofol and barbiturates all cause progressive slowing with eventual burst-suppression; dexmedetomidine may produce a pattern resembling slow-wave sleep; and ketamine may increase theta rhythms.
questions.topic: effect of sedative and anaesthetic agents on the EEG

questions.question: What does an EEG montage refer to?
options: The arrangement or configuration of electrodes
The arrangement or configuration of the wires
How to position the hat holding the electrodes
How to position the electrodes in relation to where the heart is to decrease interference
How to position the head with respect to the EEG machine
questions.explanation: An EEG montage refers to the arrangement or configuration of the recording electrodes.

questions.question: Choose which of the following could be indications for continuous EEG (cEEG).
options: Monitoring the neurological consequences of increased intracranial pressure
questions.explanation: Continuous EEG (cEEG) is indicated in non-convulsive status epilepticus, hepatic encephalopathy, cerebral ischaemia, and to monitor the neurological consequences of increased intracranial pressure - all of the listed indications apply.

questions.question: What does the EEG measure?
options: The spatial-temporal average of synchronous post-synaptic potentials among neurons
The connection between neurons and peripheral nerves
questions.explanation: The EEG measures the spatial-temporal average of synchronous post-synaptic potentials among neurons.

questions.question: What would a healthy patient's EEG look like?
options: Alpha rhythm is seen if they are awake and with eyes closed
Beta activity is seen if they are mentally active
If falling asleep, slow frequencies such as theta and delta would be seen
Alpha rhythm when awake with eyes closed, beta activity when mentally active, and theta/delta activity on falling asleep are all correct
It will depend on the age and sex of the patient
questions.explanation: In a healthy, awake patient with eyes closed, an alpha rhythm is seen; beta activity is seen when mentally active; and slow frequencies such as theta and delta appear on falling asleep.
questions.topic: normal EEG patterns by state of arousal

questions.question: Which of the following clinical scenarios have a strong recommendation for performing an EEG?

statements.label: A
statements.text: All patients with acute brain injury and unexplained persistent low consciousness

statements.label: B
statements.text: EEG should always be used to detect delayed cerebral ischaemia in comatose patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage

statements.label: C
statements.text: Patients who, after convulsive status epilepticus, do not return to functional baseline within 60 minutes, or after receiving medication

statements.label: D
statements.text: After cardiac arrest, during targeted temperature management and within 24 hours of the rewarming phase

questions.explanation: Strong recommendations for EEG include: all patients with acute brain injury and unexplained persistent low consciousness; patients who do not return to functional baseline within 60 minutes of convulsive status epilepticus, or after receiving medication; and patients after cardiac arrest, during targeted temperature management and within 24 hours of the rewarming phase. EEG should not be relied on as a blanket tool for detecting delayed cerebral ischaemia in comatose patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage - identification of DCI is an indication for perfusion CT instead. [Note: the source question offered a fifth option, 'during thrombectomy procedure in stroke patients' (also not a strong indication), which was omitted here to fit the standard four-statement format - see delivery notes.]

questions.question: Regarding MRI, which of these statements are true:

statements.label: A
statements.text: MRI is the modality of choice for the initial evaluation of TBI

statements.label: B
statements.text: MRI is indicated for ICU patients with high levels of cardio-respiratory support

statements.label: C
statements.text: MRI is indicated in metabolic diseases

statements.label: D
statements.text: MRI should not be considered in stable patients with a severe TBI

questions.explanation: CT is the imaging modality of choice for the initial evaluation of TBI, where common injuries are easily detected. ICU patients with high levels of cardio-respiratory support are an absolute contraindication for MRI. MRI should be considered in all stable patients with a severe TBI and persistent impairment of consciousness that is not explained by CT appearances or seizures, after one or two weeks.
questions.topic: indications and contraindications for MRI in TBI

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room by ambulance after a car crash. On admission, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 6. The patient is intubated and you order a CT. You receive the following image from the CT. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A subdural haematoma may appear crescent-shaped and can cross cranial sutures, because it lies below the dura; however, it will not cross the midline, as it is bound by the falx. It may extend along the falx or tentorium.

questions.question: A 23-year-old man was hit with a baseball bat during a fight. You are called to see him in the emergency room. On examination he can follow commands and has no pupillary abnormalities, and he tells you he has a terrible headache. You order a head CT. When you return from talking with the radiologist, the patient is no longer conscious, and his left pupil is mydriatic. You intubate the patient and take him for a CT. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Contusion in the left temporal lobe
Small punctate haemorrhages in the brainstem
Crescent-shaped haemorrhage in the left epidural space
Lens-shaped haemorrhage in the left epidural space
questions.explanation: The most likely finding causing this loss of consciousness is an epidural haemorrhage.

questions.question: A severe TBI patient was admitted to the ICU 10 days ago; he has no sedation and is unresponsive. After ruling out other causes, you suspect diffuse axonal injury. Which of the following neuroimaging findings will help confirm your diagnosis?

statements.label: A
statements.text: CT: punctate haemorrhages (high density) in the corpus callosum

statements.label: B
statements.text: MRI: punctate lesions in the brainstem, high signal on DWI sequence

statements.label: C
statements.text: MRI: punctate lesions at the grey/white junction, high signal on FLAIR sequence

statements.label: D
statements.text: MRI: punctate lesions in the corpus callosum, low signal on GRE sequence

questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] The source gave no explanatory feedback for this item beyond a cross-reference to its CT/MRI pathology sections, so the answer key is worth checking against the original course text if possible: punctate corpus-callosum haemorrhage on CT, grey/white-junction lesions on FLAIR MRI, and corpus-callosum lesions with low GRE signal were marked as supporting a diagnosis of diffuse axonal injury, while a brainstem lesion with high DWI signal was marked as not supporting it - which runs against standard teaching that the brainstem is one of the three classic DAI locations (with the corpus callosum and grey/white junction) and that DWI restricted diffusion is a recognised finding there too.
questions.topic: imaging findings in diffuse axonal injury

questions.question: Which of the following are indications for computed tomography?
questions.explanation: Sinus thrombosis and diffuse axonal injury are indications for MRI rather than plain CT. Identification of delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) is an indication specifically for perfusion CT, not a standard CT scan.
questions.topic: indications for CT vs MRI vs perfusion CT

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room by her husband. He states that she was normal before going to sleep, but this morning she cannot talk or walk. On examination she is aphasic and hemiplegic on her right side. Because the time of onset is unknown, you decide to perform a perfusion CT. Which of the following findings would make her a candidate for endovascular thrombolysis?
options: Decreased CBF and CBV, increased MTT
Decreased CBF, normal CBV and increased MTT
Increased CBF and CBV, decreased MTT
Increased CBF, normal CBV and decreased MTT
questions.explanation: The ischaemic penumbra - potentially salvageable tissue - is identified by decreased cerebral blood flow (CBF) with maintained cerebral blood volume (CBV) and prolonged mean transit time (MTT) extending beyond the area of established infarction (a CBV/MTT mismatch). Reference: Wing SC, Markus HS. Interpreting CT perfusion in stroke. Practical Neurology 2019;19:136.
questions.topic: perfusion CT criteria for endovascular thrombolysis candidacy
